art1.title: on play and its opposing pressures

body.text: After I helped a close friend move a couch, we collaged with a stack of magazines in the corner of their room

We cut in straight lines, not so straight lines, and around corners. So the background and foreground you see here is a scanned result of our playfulness. Play is culturally one of the most important rituals we participate in, as a young child, as a teenager, as an adult, with community, and to learn countless lessons. I recently took a visit to the [Noguchi Museum](https://www.noguchi.org/), a museum in Long Island City dedicated to the works and life of acclaimed sculptor [Isamu Noguchi](https://www.noguchi.org/isamu-noguchi/biography/biography/). Past the beautifully green and peaceful garden, up the stairs in the back of the first floor, I came across one of his greatest unrealized works: [Play Mountain](https://www.noguchi.org/artworks/collection/view/play-mountain/).

Pitched to New York City’s Park Commissioner [Robert Moses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses) in 1934, Noguchi proposed an incredibly grand and bold transformation of a city block within Central Park, a building structured like a huge pyramid. It would be far from an ordinary building, but a playground with countless steps reaching the top of the contraption, and long-winding slides sloping down to the base. Noguchi envisioned children water-tubing down the slides in the summer and sledding down the slides in the winter. It is purposefully left without many instructions, so anyone could use their imaginations to unlock infinite ways to engage with the space and explore. Noguchi Museum’s senior curator Dakin Hart explains in [this article](https://www.grimshaw.foundation/stories/noguchi-s-playscapes), 'Noguchi had a really good concept that playgrounds should not be designed like military exercise equipment for a cheaply executed boot camp'.

When Play Mountain was presented to Robert Moses, he crushed the idea underfoot, citing the structure’s lack of practicality and usefulness. The famed and controversial city planner used utility as an opposing pressure, as a dream killer for Noguchi. When I was looking at the unrealized model at the museum, I couldn't help but feel a sense of loss, to not be able to sled down the hypothetical slope in winter. This is only one example of practicality fighting against creative exploration. What other opposing pressures do I experience when it comes to play? Do I even play at all, at the ripe age of 25?
I believe that true play, creativity for the sake of creativity, is actually really hard to produce

Even the word I just used there, ‘produce’, makes me stop and think about how there’s an implication of an end output to be produced and profited off of.  I’ve been reading [Free Play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Play:_Improvisation_in_Life_and_Art), a book about living a life of creative improvisation by Stephen Nachmanovich, where he mentions the Hindu concept of [‘lila’](https://www.embodiedphilosophy.com/what-is-lila/), which roughly translates to ‘divine play’. This is unencumbered creativity, freedom from the pressure of a finished state, strengthened by the spontaneity and the joy of the process itself.

I see ‘pressure’ as the main obstacle to free creativity. Pressure from the four walls of your mind, pressure to improve through practice, pressure to perform and be seen performing, and the pressure to support yourself in a capitalist society. In fact, I think it takes a high level of discipline to notice those pressures, let them pass through you like a river, and relax. The need for discipline seems paradoxical to the act of letting go.
The pressure to perfectly fit your creativity in a package and deliver it to the world feels all-encompassing

This example of pressure is the biggest one stopping me from truly valuing my creativity as something to enjoy on its own rather than as a means to an end. One of the biggest questions I catch myself asking about prospective projects is: “How would this look or translate in my portfolio?”. This immediately shifts my frame of thinking into imagining the end result and its benefits or costs, rather than committing to the intricate steps of creation. I don’t really blame myself for falling into this rat trap, because of the huge societal pressure placed on the design portfolio (unless I’m wrong and I should blame myself, let me know!). It feels like the portfolio is the expected vehicle a designer drives to creative success, or employment. We move in a delicate performance, to supposedly communicate the perfect balance between unique, efficient, and creative in a business-friendly way.  As if I’m chatting with a prospective employer and saying: 'Yes, I’m talented and also perfectly positioned to make your C-suite more money'.
Is it impossible to play if it doesn’t feel fun to make what you’re making?

I’d say that a huge characteristic of play is that it’s fun, it’s joyful, it’s a moment you disappear into and stash away your sense of time. However, if I’m designing for the web, making a poster, or writing an essay, I wouldn’t describe it as fun. The first description that actually popped into my head is ‘necessary’. So in that way, creation feels like a lot more of a serious act to me. To go back to Nachmanovitch’s Free Play, he mentions a perspective of creativity, where the act of making art actually sands away the rough edges of who you are in order to reveal the true self. I’ve related that the work that I do, and how it feels very necessary to keep sanding.  That perspective feels a lot more hopeful to me because it implies that the most fulfilled creative we want to be is already living in a home inside of us, waiting for the doorbell to be rung.

On a more existentially confusing side of the coin – I feel like if I don’t consistently write, read, make weird posters, or engage critically, I’m always at risk of losing my mind to the abyss of endless scrolling, short-form Instagram content, and fruitless comparisons to other people’s work. The shovel is in my hands, and now I need to dig out the filling hole of dirt that is flattening all of us against the earth. Playing, moving my hands both in the digital and physical realm, feels absolutely essential to remember my own identity in a world while creativity is being automated away.

So if we go back to the term ‘necessary’, then that invokes an image of scratching an itch, unclogging a stream of flowing water.  I frequently return to an [interview](https://thecreativeindependent.com/people/artist-technologist-and-researcher-matthew-prebeg-on-prioritizing-play/) between [The Creative Independent](https://thecreativeindependent.com/) and [Matthew Prebeg](https://matt-prebeg.com/), a Toronto-based technologist and researcher. He bases his play off of endless curiosity, consistently asking questions, and unraveling the strings until they fray. He adds this thought on play: “I get excited to think about a world where different rules apply, where we can challenge the way we understand things and imagine different futures. Play is political in that sense”. So in that framework, if we use play to rearrange and deconstruct rules around the world we understand today (this again invokes the definition of ‘lila’), play is necessary like an act of resistance.
But before we worried about pressure, before we even walked, we were masters of play

I recently spent time with my young nephew and niece. They took me by the hand, asked me to play toy cars with them. We made the plastic cars do backflips, engage in races, engage in chases. They sat me down in a side chair, placing me in their make-believe restaurant and told me to order anything from the menu. I wanted steak (sorry to all my vegans), and then hot chocolate. With our young malleable and sponge-soaking minds, we all did this, we constructed worlds.

I don’t agree with saying something like ‘we just need to unlock our inner child!’. To me, that implies that we should tune out the noise, the scary, the bad. I actually think that when we try to play, we should acknowledge everything about the pressure cooker that we live in.  For example, journaling by hand for fun despite the fact that thoughts can be molded and generated with the click of a button. Finding joy (or if not joy, at least satisfaction) within those constraints is powerful.
I maintain a shared digital photo album for my partner, called 'cherry blossoms'.

Photos from that album are scattered around this rose, collected from my early spring walks around the neighborhood. Cherry blossoms in New York are fleeting, ephemeral, present for a moment or two, and then you have to wait until next year to take a photo to add to a shared album or any album for that matter.
The web feels similar in that way, littered with fleeting cultural moments in time.

Everyone who expresses themselves on the web finds a personal corner amidst infinite space, and calls it a ‘site’. I’m really interested in peoples’ descriptions of what the digital web means to them, different definitions of how it molds the world around us. [Laurel Swchulst](https://laurelschwulst.com/home/) describes her own website as ‘[a shifting house](https://laurelschwulst.com/e/my-website-is-a-shifting-house/) next to a river of knowledge’. [Maggie Appleton](https://maggieappleton.com/) talks about personal information, knowledge, and expression like tending to your garden, [‘a collection of evolving ideas’](https://maggieappleton.com/garden-history). I feel obligated to get in on the fun and describe the ways that I see existence on the web, thinking beyond the current flattening of corporatized and AI-powered design.
Websites are a show of vulnerability

Anyone who puts their name on a website, and makes it publicly available, is practicing a scary brand of vulnerability. Especially people practicing forms of creativity. Creative websites are pored over with a fine comb, turned over and over, people expecting an endlessly smooth stone and looking for the tiniest of cracks. So I think that having a personal website is an act of bravery, which should be celebrated regardless of what 'state' it’s in. I think no matter how confident you are in your skills, you feel that vulnerability as a result of the flowing stream of feedback, thoughts, comments, and concerns. The difference, probably, is in how comfortable you feel with that.
Websites are a steady stream of growth

This feels more attuned to personal websites than any random website, but bear with me. When we grab a corner of digital real estate, we curate the ways we want to express ourselves, and it feels like there are infinite ways to do so. But websites are a snapshot in time, the way that we choose to communicate in the moment, “Here I am, and here’s what I’m about”. I see some websites have archive sections, collecting past versions of itself and showcasing change over time. I think that adjusting layouts, switching color schemes, updating projects from old to new, or editing the way we describe ourselves on the web, is always a sign of growth. Whether those changes make the website 'better' or not, is murky and subjective. But if you maintain a website, changing any aspect of it feels like growth because you’re making a calculated decision on if how you visually represent yourself on the web aligns with who you are in the moment.
Websites are an act of protest

In the year 2026, the web is hurtling down a highway of more AI slop, more optimization, more corporatized minimalism, and less weird ideas. I believe that any website that is designed in opposition to that is a form of protest. I think that websites existing just for the sake of being there, rather than addressing a business need or problem, is a form of protest. What do we materially gain when we visit [this website](http://yeahlemons.com/) where a bunch of lemons endlessly fall from the sky? How about [here](https://www.iamaturtle.org/), where the phrase “I am a turtle” is translated 80 different ways? (Source: [Mimi Reyburn’s](https://mimireyburn.com/Hey%2C+I'm+Mimi!) collection of [useless websites](https://mimireyburn.com/Misc./Mimi's+Website+Collection#**Genuinely+Useless**)). Nothing, from the lens of “productivity” or “better output”, but personally it makes me feel more grounded knowing that ideas are limitless and people are grabbing unique ones every day.
Websites are a gift to give

A close friend of mine shared a Valentine’s Day website she made on [Hotglue](https://hotglue.me/), a web publishing tool which feels like you’re making a collage. Its’ sole purpose was to wish our group a happy Valentine’s Day. I saw a [reel](https://www.instagram.com/p/DULtwWikSTA/) where someone coded a website specifically to ask his girlfriend if she would be his Valentine, a true yearner and a real one. It’s possible to build digital worlds as a form of gift giving, a token of celebration and thoughtful appreciation. I really love the term [“pebbling”](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pebbling), which Wikipedia describes as “the act of offering small, meaningful objects or gestures to establish social bonds”. There are two species of penguins where a male gifts a female a stone. They keep gifting each other stones, until they have enough to build a nest for themselves and future offspring. In the past few years, this term has gained meaning in a digital sense, as we share memes and reels to people we care about. Can a shared website be a form of pebbling? Make a website wishing your friends a good morning! Make your mom a Mother’s Day website! Make a website inviting people over to dinner!
The negative connotations surrounding the web feel overwhelming

I can speak in vague metaphors about websites all I want, but the truth is more and more people want to be offline. People are abandoning the high-powered machines in their pockets, and the intelligence they carry, in favor of flip phones. I feel like there’s a nefarious wheel spinning, containing nodes of connection between the web, tech, AI, social media, reduced attention span, and doom scrolling addiction. I could throw a number of other scary phrases into the mix here. Reading this might be another form of consumption. Maybe we need to burn down the web instead of trying to add to it. I believe there’s a balancing act needed, where we can identify positive digital experiences of warmth, while stewarding moments of criticism. It might be easier to be offline though, I can’t argue against that.
here’s a question i never stop asking myself, one which hangs on to me like a child with their parent on the first day of pre-school.

what does it mean to be “great” at something? a great artist, writer, companion, friend, talker, listener, or anything in between. or simply good enough? what a confusing and subjective term, similar to words like “taste”, “craft”, and “intuition”.  i believe that understanding grows with the act of repetition, practicing and noticing details over and over again.  when it comes to art and writing i hurl words and an artwork-filled 1080 by 1080 pixel box into the digital void, searching for some sort of universal nod of approval while at the same time fearing the act of asking for it.  i’m not sure where I look for confirmation and validation, but at the same time i’m certain that i’m searching for it everywhere.  for this specific photo, i texted my girlfriend a screenshot and said, “look I added lasers lol”. she hasn’t responded. it’s also currently very early in the morning for her, in france.
i took a class in college that set out to answer the question of what makes design good.

here were some commonly mentioned words: design principles, style, balance, eurocentrism.  actually, one of the overarching messages of the class was that all roads lead to eurocentrism. but to my memory, i don’t think we crossed the chasm of finding out how to believe our own work was good. it was always about how to interpret the quality of what everyone else was making, or how others can interpret the quality of what you were making.  at that point, i guess we’d be walking on the sword’s edge between design theory and critique, and therapy. there’s probably some shit about this in the artist’s way (that one super popular creativity book) in the first two chapters. i’d barely know cause I only read the first two chapters. i think i’m supposed to start a book club on it soon, which is an exciting prospect.
i also recently explored paul graham’s article on what it means to do great work, past simply working hard.

it feels like rather than exploring a few central themes on the topic, he sequentially explores multiple small themes which relate to each other and build over the course of the essay. he explores a wide range, from how to find out what you want to be great at, to how to pursue your chosen field consistently, to how curiosity leads to originality. something that just caught my eye right now and resonated with me: “people who do great things don't get a lot done every day. they get something done, rather than nothing”. my brother told my mom this once, and i’m not sure if he got it from somewhere else, that the most beneficial workout you can do is one you can do consistently. here’s a point i did not see explicitly mentioned in the article though, it’s super helpful to believe that you are even capable of making great work in the first place. that belief is an everyday conscious decision. it feels important to believe that your progress is strong enough to be critiqued by other people, and that even if the perception of quality from an outside perspective isn’t as strong as your own perception, then you have the skills to improve your work.
i grew up in a super competitive schooling system, and its social norms told me to look at everything through the lens of excellence.

reflecting on that experience has brought up another critical question: is greatness and achievement always the point? somewhere along the way, i probably lost the ability to occasionally look at creation as an act of play with no functional outcome. to create, drift in the mist, and not think about “what should I do with this”, is a joy. also, there are probably more important things to think about (and act on) than my creative angst. for example: the burning world, our responsibility to said world, the hopes that we carry in our hearts, and the systemic fires that set out to scorch them. we have obligations past our own desires and goals.
This artwork demonstrates a masterful command of technique and vision.
The intricate details

reveal themselves gradually, inviting close examination. The work speaks to themes of memory, identity, and the passage of time, creating a rich tapestry of meaning for those who engage with it deeply.
My close friend texted me a link to a Brazilian samba funk album that they thought I’d enjoy

Maria Fumaca was Banda Black Rio’s first funk / jazz album released in 1977, and became one of the most influential Brazilian funk albums of the last century. My friend saw a lot of parallels in Masayoshi Takanaka’s music, who for us has some of the most otherworldly and eclectic rock of all time (who else is playing shows with a giant surfboard electric guitar?). But I have a terrible confession to make: after my first listen, I was actually kind of indifferent to Maria Fumaca itself. Maybe I need to cleanse my musical palate, or maybe I need to give the album another chance, but the comparison to Takanaka by my friend actually just made me want to listen to Takanaka. I have the tendency to replay the music that I love into oblivion.

However, I was so inspired by Maria Fumaca’s album art: the circular gathering of the band members, the shadowy figures, the movement of the dynamic typography. It was weird in a way that I liked my posters to be weird, and I thought I’d be able to add something of my own with the way I use textures and color. Being inspired is a tricky game, because what do we do with the abundance of information soup that we are fed everyday for breakfast, lunch, and dinner? We scroll and tap through digital worlds, we see and hear snippets of people’s thoughts literally all the time, and the algorithm churns the butter of content. How do we parse through the work and thinking that inspire us, and leave what doesn’t at the door? And once we get to what moves us, how do we take action in our own work?
I made this poster to welcome my partner to NYC after two and a half years of long distance.
Coincidentally, i made this on my two year anniversary of living in new york. So, a meaningful time, for both of us.
I made this a long time ago, but it's always given me a similar feeling

There are a lot of ways I’ve interpreted how this man feels: sitting in his dark room, lights off, only the TV glow present. In the past, I’ve related the picture to how I feel under the weight of productivity, and the need to perform as a designer for a hypothetical and omnipresent audience. The weight of consistent output and good work. This has felt even more apparent as it becomes seemingly easier and easier to build with LLM-powered tools.
I walk on a tightrope of contradictions

I have trained for a job which directs people to 'be online', in a world where people are waking up and realizing that their desires do not lie behind a phone or a computer screen. Gen Z is increasingly choosing to remove smart phones (with all its attention control and data mining) from their lives, swapping them out with the Nokias and the Motorolas of old. Words like 'stakeholder', 'user', 'q1', and 'fiscal year' dance in and out of my mouth, words that ring hollow outside of corporate design. [David Graeber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Graeber) talks about this idea that corporate overlords decided that we would use such jargon, in his collection of essays ['The Utopia of Rules'](https://theanarchistlibrary.org/library/david-graeber-the-utopia-of-rules). Yet within the storm of design flows, more optimization, more output, I'd still like to sift through the noise and slop and improve my 'craft'.
But the word 'craft' also lies in a bed of contradictions

For a product designer, it pops up everywhere, as some godly idea. everyone wants designers to understand craft, to hold nuanced understandings of visual beauty and make good decisions in the increasingly large sea of options. ‘Perfect your craft’, ’wield your craft’, ‘hone your craft’, as if i need to have some earth-scorching weapon to go to war with. As a professional, craft demands precision with unwavering intentionality. Yet, we don’t always have to consider this practice in such a intense way.

Crafting can be interpreted as play without strict rules, messing around with physical or digital objects that aren’t bound by our needs for perfection. There are of course, master craftsmen who hone metaphorically and literally (like blades and such), racking up their 10,000 hours of perfection. To me, it feels like saying: ‘now is my time to craft’ refers to a more relaxing kind of activity. If we allow ourselves to see it that way. Because that is easier said than done. For example, I’ve tried crocheting and instead of feeling relaxed I’ve instead felt deep rage.

But an even more ironic part of perfecting your craft: improvement requires us to pay attention to a million small details, in a world where our attention spans are getting closer and closer to zero. The endless scroll, the weapon wielded to perfection to boost user engagement, has a hold on me and doesn’t let go. If someone asked me to describe, I don’t know, a pencil for more than 30 seconds, could I? Could I describe with detail how the object appeals to my five senses, in what way, why and how? Maybe for like 15, perhaps. I worry that with the ability to quickly summarize anything and everything around us, we will lose the ability to dig deep on a topic, to rabbit-hole, to go through a door in our peripheral view because of the hallway that we previously walked through.
Will a designer always be in a conflict of morality?

This is one of my biggest contradictions: I want to do creative work that feels fulfilling in a system where moral ambiguity looms large. Of course, this is a tale as old as time (or at least as old as the rise of corporate capitalism). I constantly revisit the words of [Elizabeth Goodspeed](https://elizabethgoodspeed.com/) in her [article](https://www.itsnicethat.com/features/is-there-such-thing-as-an-ethical-designer-creative-industry-280825) for the creative newsletter [‘It’s Nice That’](https://www.itsnicethat.com/), where she muses about how possible it is to truly be an ethical designer in a swirling storm of the cost of living, uncertainty, loss of culture and identity, and pressure to inject AI into every aspect of our being. I particularly enjoy repeating one phrase from that article to my friends and to myself: ‘Only the unemployed are ethical’. It’s feeling less like a joke and more of a certainty.

The heart of this contradiction lies within the way designers are trained versus what’s actually rewarded today in the tech world. Designers learn to consistently pause and question, ask why, ask if what they are told to design is the right thing to build. However, the most dominant technologies that are grabbing the space in front of us are built with this attitude: “ask questions later, build the product first, build the data center first, use the world’s resources first”. [Sam Kriss](https://substack.com/@samkriss) has a humorous and bleak [analysis](https://harpers.org/archive/2026/03/childs-play-sam-kriss-ai-startup-roy-lee/) of the San-Francisco based ‘20-something founder attitude’, an article I consistently return to and think about. Already jumping out on first load, the article’s subtitle is: ‘Tech’s new generation and the end of thinking’. He points out a new perception in Big Tech and Silicon Valley, that the greatest quality which will save from the 'permanent underclass' is 'agency', which is the ability to do anything without asking or waiting for permission. He centers this sentiment around the story of [Roy Lee](https://www.linkedin.com/in/roy-lee-goat/) and [Cluely](https://cluely.com/), which he started when he was suspended from Columbia after posting a video of him cheating on an Amazon coding interview. When I navigated to the open roles section of Cluely’s job page, it yelled at me: ‘You're running out of time to make generational wealth. This is your best shot”. Ideally, this is not the type of behavior that gets rewarded, but Cluely has received millions in funding from venture capitalist firms. Questionable actions being rewarded heavily in the startup world is absolutely not a new idea, but it feels incredibly amplified in the AI era.
What would it mean to explore alternate pathways?

I am absolutely not the first person to ask questions like these. I am continuously inspired by many designers and design organizations who have faced the machine and have still found a sense of fulfillment and satisfaction in the work that they do (at least from an outside perspective, it SEEMS like some designers have cracked the morality code, I am not in anyone’s head nor ever will I ever be in anyone’s head but my own). I’ve been interested in creative / designer cooperatives, which are an alternative away from corporate hierarchical structures of large enterprises and lean startups. I myself lived in a housing co-op in Austin, Texas, so I was pretty psyched to learn about the company version of that.

Co-ops are worker owned, which means that all designers in the co-op govern the business together and benefit equally. These are the type of spaces that have bylaws, codes of conduct, and shared visions on how designers can achieve equitable futures together. Is AI an inevitable force of efficiency, a sweeping wave to overtake all other forms of creation? Tech researcher Ayla Ahmed from the remote tech cooperative, [Sassafras Tech Collective](https://sassafras.coop/), punches back on this notion by stating in this blog article that using AI gives workers a perception that they are working faster, but actually their time is being diverted into prompting and prompt tweaking. The fact that the article exists is my most important takeaway. Sassafras is a tech workplace that critically examines the role of AI in everyday technology development, rather than being a corporation that uses AI to chase after profit margins and max out token usage. You can find a much more extensive list of tech co-ops [here](https://tech-coops.xyz/).

In Brooklyn, I turn towards [Partner and Partners](https://partnerandpartners.com/) as a north star of high quality work, high profile clients, and principled ethics. Also in Brooklyn, the non-profit design studio [Public Policy Lab](https://www.publicpolicylab.org) delivers complex and thorough work across multiple policy areas while maintaining a commitment to high visual craft. And while [Studio Rodrigo](https://www.studiorodrigo.com/) is not a worker-owned co-op, I’ve read some blogs and thinking from their founder Ritik Dholakia, and it seems like the studio itself grapples with being ethical designers and delivering craft-filled work to the right clients. This feels evident in his [2025 reflection](https://ritikdholakia.medium.com/2025-rate-of-change-1cf08985d3e7) on work that they’ve accomplished along with what they wrestle with in the midst of advancing technology. And here’s a huge coincidence, check out this roundtable on how creative co-ops work, including Partner and Partners and moderated by Dholakia (I was going to go in-person but then I got sick, sadly).

Although the existence of co-ops and these other design studios give me hope, working in the world that we live in is never that straight-forward. I do try to not put things and people on a pedestal. There's a reason why 'never meet your heroes' is a phrase. Being the most ethical designer in the world doesn’t pay your rent, and sticking to your principles as a design firm does not protect you from the realities of running a small business. But that doesn’t mean the alternatives don’t exist, and that we can’t attempt to find balance in the gray.
Sharing something personal, like art, writing, and thoughts, feels like putting your head through a guillotine.

It’s an offering, it’s a revelation of self, to anyone who wants to observe or just walk past. You kneel there, your head through the hole, waiting for someone to bring down the appendage that cuts off heads. I have no idea what it’s called. But I’m hoping that in the act of doing so, I feel more comfortable doing it. I am hoping the guillotine hole becomes a friend, and the neck that’s being severed hardens a little, becomes a malleable metal. Thanks for indulging me on this.
I made a poster for a holiday party I’m hosting soon with my roommates

I’m lucky enough to say that since I moved to New York, we’ve been able to host gatherings very consistently! It seems that cooking for 120 housemates in college has given me the ability to cut an onion and the inability to make smaller portions. It gives me comfort, combining the friends that you know separately, having them come together, and making bonds that might not involve you at all. It’s the whole cog in the system thing, not the capitalist predatory kind. sometimes it feels like we exist as these cogs, allowing others to connect and turn each other as part of a non-oppressive machine. It feels kind of dramatic to insinuate that I’m responsible for this, but then sometimes it feels bigger than just the opportunity to hang out with my friends. It’s part of the social dance that we all do, talking about our stresses and victories, sharing mutuals, sharing stories, sharing pieces of ourselves, being a body next to and around another body. Sometime during this convoluted dance, we feel like we twirl ourselves back to the guillotine, because of the vulnerability of revealing our nuances, the universes in ourselves. that’s something we accept. Being able to make a small contribution to this system encourages me to host dinner parties every month or so.
So this poster is how I invited my friends to my birthday party.

well, not completely because in my invite i fit my address in there, which i am not sharing here. i am a huge fan of oversharing but i do have some sense of boundaries. turning 24 was like a shrug of the shoulders. however, turning 25 sent me deep into the shadow realm of overthinking. it is such a problematically sandwiched number, as close to 30 as it is to 20. a true cause for a quarter-life crisis. i have metaphorically and literally been looking at myself in the mirror, because i’ve noticed a bald spot forming. when you’re a professional athlete, it is usually around now that you plateau athletically. luckily, i am nowhere near a professional athlete in any capacity, and the mind operates differently than the body. but as a product designer and a creative, i am considering this question: am i as good as i’ll ever be at design? in this period in time, is there a treadmill in the middle of a plateau that i’m running on?
the short answer: absolutely not!
I usually make all of my posters in Photoshop, but this is the first time I’ve combined assets from other creation tools

For the sky, I used [Paper](https://paper.design/) to create a default grain gradient and played around with its colors, shape, intensity, and noise. Then I dropped the moon into [Unicorn Studio](https://www.unicorn.studio/) where I added filters such as bloom, chromatic aberration, and dither. Both of these tools are primarily for building on the web, but it was nice to refashion them for my own purposes.
It is overwhelming how many tools we have access to

I’m sure you feel the weight of every single digital productivity and/or creation tool that is peddled around, AI-powered or not. Or, as an extension, literally the endless amount of streaming sites, or dating apps, or whatever service behind your personal rectangular collection of pixels will finally solve whatever problem you’re facing. There’s a reason why posts like [these](https://www.tumblr.com/orcboxer/745857099387584512/have-you-seen-the-new-show-its-on-tubu-its) crack me up. It’s not a unique situation though, for a designer’s dominant tool to change over time. People were designing interfaces in Photoshop, and then in Sketch, and then Adobe XD. I started practicing UX Design in height of Figma’s adoption. but now, with the advent of LLMs, not only is the dominant tool threatening to change again, it feels like there’s an explosion of the possible tools available. There’s Cursor, or Claude, or Codex for coding, but then also Pencil or Subframe to seamlessly blend design and code, but then also Rive for animations. I do believe that endless tool options are distractions from solid creative fundamentals. I’d like to be in the habit of asking myself more, what can I with less tools, with less power? (I understand the irony of statement considering i used 3 tools to make 1 poster).
Powerful work arises when we constrain ourselves

I will say that I am not the best voice for this thought, because letting my posters run away with textures and filters is one of my favorite things to do. I am guilty of believing that putting grain on any poster will solve all aesthetic issues.  I do think it’s a really important thought that I’d like to adopt more, considering how now it feels like you can take an idea into an existing product with the literal snap of a finger. As designers, we are trained to question why we would make or create something, which sometimes feels like has been hurled out the window considering the new tools that product designers are expected to use. I’ve seen building and coding be described in today’s age as ‘low cost’, which is very untrue considering that the cost is actually very high for the environment and the global South.

Constraints can be applied to techniques. My typography professor at UT Austin, [Kelcey Gray](https://kelceygray.com/), gave us some assignments that denied us the use of color, the use of textures, or the use of filters. It was purposeful, so that we’d block out the noise and focus on fundamentals, like pairing the right typefaces, balancing composition, subtly shifting kerning, or nudging line heights. If our attention is consumed by more and more tools, and more and more possibilities, we can lose sight of what we trained in the first place.
[Permacomputing](https://permacomputing.net/) offers a way to constrain technology itself

Applying constraints on our technology itself feels even more pressing, especially when we come back to the idea of ‘low cost technology’ versus ‘high cost technology’. Both the world’s hardware and software are built with the assumption of unlimited resources and the insatiable hunger for unlimited scale. With technological tools, fish swim in ponds only to be consumed by bigger, badder sharks. iPhones package countless natural resources only for the consumer to turn to the newer one in a few years or so.  Modern computing tools are made to die. What does it look like when we turn away, as much as possible, from all-powerful and consumption-heavy technology in favor of computing that embraces limitations and constraints?

This is where permacomputing blooms. Permacomputing is a sustainable approach to computation and network technologies which emphasizes maximizing hardware lifespans, minimizing energy use, and cultivating a healthy relationship with our environment and its resources.  This ideology is based off the idea of [‘permaculture’](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permaculture), which is an agriculture practice that creates long-lasting ecosystems of nature. The wiki for permacomputing specifically mentions the power of constraints when talking about the principle of [‘Hope for the Best, Prepare for the Worst’](https://permacomputing.net/hope_for_the_best_prepare_for_the_worst/). Permacomputing not only believes that applying constraints and limitations on the technology we use is necessary, but those constraints sharpen creativity, adaptability, and resilience. I strongly believe in the need for resiliency, despite the conveyor belt of endless digital tool options, to find your own answers and visual solutions by examining the set of principles that you live and design by.

How does this translate to the world of design? Hannah Gmeiner, a talented graphic designer, explored the idea of “Permacomputing as a practice for digital Graphic Design” as her Bachelor’s [thesis](https://permacomputingasapracticefordigitalgraphicdesign.com/). One of her explorations involve her designing posters on a miniscule 24 by 34 pixel canvas, to push back on the notion that tiny and energy-friendly files will inherently be pixelated and aesthetically unappealing. She primarily used a vector-based program and exported her work as a PDF rather than using a large file-size format of a JPG or a PNG.  This work is actually in direct opposition to…my own design practice!  After learning more about permacomputing and Gmeiner’s work, I’ve realized how much bloat my Photoshop files hold, a hot air balloon of pixels floating away from me, not curated with the care it needs. I am excited to put these concepts into my own poster / art making process. My personal favorite line from Gmeiner’s thoughts on permacomputing: 'The principle behind designing with Permacomputing principles is that there is a place for everything. No tools or design practices are superfluous or irrelevant. There is room for both slow and fast, for incremental and one-off processes.'
Do we really need to optimize everything?

Completely unrelated fact: I enjoy journaling a lot. I write in a green leather notebook, recently acquired after I finished my red notebook (which took 13 months to get all the way through). I appreciate them because the musings inside of them are artifacts of consistency. I have just started a new notebook, called my “structured list” notebook. I am only allowed to create to-do lists of checkboxes inside of them. I am not allowed to have any free-flowing unstructured writing in there. I create 3 or 4 to-do items per day, and I don’t religiously maintain it. Is there a more optimized way to have to-do lists? There most certainly is. But I know that I am consistent with unstructured journaling, so I’m confident that I will enjoy this new notebook more than having a Notion table or a Kanban grid.

The idea of having an analog solution rather than a digital solution directly correlates to another permacomputing principle: [Not Doing](https://permacomputing.net/not_doing/). The power behind ‘not doing’ something is that we pause, critically reflect, and ask ourselves what is needed in the moment. The question that goes beyond the question of, “do I need a digital solution?” is something like “do I even need to do anything at all?”. We’ve come back full circle to directly face the popular, age-old tech mantra of “move fast and break things”.  The tech worker’s metric of success is one of efficiency, the speed of shipping, how fast a product or feature goes to market. It almost feels more radical to sit there for an extended second, not make that app, not make that next thing immediately, especially in a time in history where creating and accessing technology seems as easy as it’s ever been.
Our own set of principles can help us pick the tools we care about
